items.summary: 米ニューヨーク州立大学ストーニーブルック校に所属する研究者らが発表した論文「Penny for Your Prompts: A Measurement Study of Contextual Leakage in AI Chat Platforms」（IEEE S&P 2027採択）は、AIチャットbotに入力した会話内容や個人情報が、サイト内の追跡プログラム（トラッカー）を通じて外部企業へ漏えいする実態を調査した研究報告だ。
items.titleJa: AIに打ち明けた相談は“広告トラッカー”に筒抜け？ ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini含む42サービスを米大が調査
items.summaryJa: AIチャットボットへの入力内容や個人情報が、サイト内のトラッカーを介して外部企業へ漏えいする実態を、42サービスを対象に調査した結果、21サービスで会話の要約タイトルが送信され、9サービスではプロンプトがそのまま送信されていたことが分かった。汎用AIでは約22%の外部通信がトラッカー向けで、送信先はGoogleが41.8%と最も多く、次いでMicrosoft、ByteDance、Metaの順だった。漏えいの原因は、トラッカーがWebページのタイトルを自動取得する機能をそのまま動かしているためで、プロンプト本文や会話の核心はページ名として読み取られ外部へ送信される流れが確認された。

items.title: Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start

items.title: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
items.summary: Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway . Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs , and observability as catalog models , so every model your team uses is managed in one place. Use Private Inference to: Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID. Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider. Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway. Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs , trace drains , and custom reporting . Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model. Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails. To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves. items.title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
items.summary: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done. Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery , Selection , Access , and Success . You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly. That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one. The agentic testing pyramid If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid , the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite. To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success , that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome. An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench , are E2E evals. Example Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans . Here’s a typical request from one of your customers: Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission. Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am: Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature) 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget) Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time) Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three) Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans : How to build an end-to-end eval We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor , an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions. Here are the terms we’ll use: Task : one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded Variant : the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills Trial : one attempt by one variant at one task Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output Step 1: Set a goal Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier ). Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places: Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate For example, your goal might be to: Increase the success rate on a specific task Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it A/B test a prompt Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why Example We looked in all three places for sfbeans : Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness. Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added. Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn. That gives us our goal: Goal Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for Agents Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from. In scope Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans . Out of scope Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later. Done when Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time. Step 2: Define metrics Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals: Success Success rate: the share of trials that pass Pass@k : the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”) Pass^k : the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”) Efficiency (measured on successful trials only) Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task Time: how long the trial took Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars Example Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ( anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway ) on the iced latte order could look like: Trial Result What happened Steps Time Cost 1 Pass Compared quotes from 3 cafes, ordered at Valencia 9 3:40 $0.52 2 Fail: over budget Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27 5 1:50 $0.31 3 Pass Compared quotes from 4 cafes, ordered at Valencia 11 4:30 $0.68 4 Fail: late Ordered at Dolores, ready 9:20 6 2:10 $0.35 5 Pass Skipped Fog City, ordered at Valencia 8 3:20 $0.49 What the numbers mean: Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%. Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once. Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right. Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials. Time: ~3:50 on successful trials. Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too. So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time . Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5. Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters: Product What a failed attempt costs the user Metric to lead with Order my morning coffee Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust Pass^k Coding agent with a test suite Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again Pass@k Draft an email the user reviews A quick edit before hitting send Success rate Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.” Step 3: Design the task set In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for. Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act. For each task, define these parts: An instruction: the user’s request An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent. Example We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/ . Common case: iced-latte-mission , the order from earlier Edge case: usual-unavailable , where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink Edge case: team-order , with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot Don’t act: impossible-request , where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5). Here’s iced-latte-mission : The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection , keeping the eval focused on Success . We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time: The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning: To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly. For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json : The actual check lives in check_orders.py . It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score: The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works: Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5: Step 4: Run the eval If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each. Harbor’s Vercel integration , which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox , and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers. Example Two agents, Claude Code and Codex , with two models each, make four variants. Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job: This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 ( Sandbox limits ). To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway. Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment. Step 5: Analyze traces Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied. Example The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/ . Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed: Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative). For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally. Variant Success Pass^5 Avg steps (successful) Cost per success (incl. failed trials) Claude Code + Opus 5.5 85% 60% 9 $0.61 Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 75% 52% 11 $0.27 Codex + GPT-6 Astra 80% 43% 8 $0.48 Codex + GPT-6.1 Sol 65% 14% 13 $0.22 That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials. Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke: Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json . The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order . No quote . It treated the menu price as the final price. Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money. We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.” When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring: Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO. Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one. Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins. Automated trace analysis For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it. Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs. Model calls go through AI Gateway . Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage. Iterate to greatness Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it. Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship. Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it. Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next. Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again . Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace. items.title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
items.summary: When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits. Last year, we shipped just that , with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it. More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged. The first is automation : Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines. The second is agents and harnesses : Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too. As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance. Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three. More secure workflows The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection. Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end , before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools. Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change: Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log. Encryption on self-hosted Worlds Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams. A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management . Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay: More security work in v5 Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads. You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0 , inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability. A redesigned trace viewer The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development. Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets. Workflows in every region In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1 . Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress. For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region . Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path. By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration: To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start() . That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay: The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1 . Infrastructure reliability Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover. With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors. As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug. Agent-ready performance In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today. Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit. In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes. The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures. Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers: Fewer queue hops In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout. The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms . Incremental replay Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log : replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms . The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes. WebSocket streaming Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default . In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds . Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression. These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application. Benchmark results and methodology Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1 , against the managed Vercel World . Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out. Selected results · v4.8.12 compared with v5.2.0 Measurement v4.8.12 v5.2.0 Change First step, p75 418 ms 172 ms 2.4× faster Between steps, p75 618 ms 109 ms 5.7× faster Late-run overhead, p75 1,748 ms 70 ms 25× lower 1,020 steps, median 21.0 min 3.0 min 7× faster Resume, p75 699 ms 425 ms 1.6× faster Stream delivery, median 226.1 s 53.5 s 4.2× faster Chunk trip time, p75 172 ms 102 ms 1.7× faster Runs with a chunk delayed >1 s 6 / 10 0 / 10 100% fewer The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation . Worlds: the shared durability primitive Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World : the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness , which adds durability to existing agent harnesses. Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness. Choose the integration around how you want to build: Workflow SDK : write durable application logic with use workflow and use step . WorkflowAgent : use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow. fx : embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx. durable-harness : keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it. Supports Pi and OpenCode , with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox. eve : build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds. We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability. items.titleJa: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
items.summaryJa: Workflow SDK 5は、クラッシュやデプロイ後も長時間待機するワークフローを安定して動かすことを目的としている。暗号化機能を強化し、全ペイロードをAES-256-GCMでエンドツーエンド保護、デプロイ時に復号可能、Vercel上では追加設定不要でキーはデプロイごとに導出される。また、地域分散によって各ランが開始地域を中心にデータを保持し、クロスリージョンの負荷を低減。可観測性は従来通り維持され、トレースビューアの刷新やラン属性の追加、ポリシーとしてのペイロード保持制御など、セキュリティと信頼性、パフォーマンスの向上を図っている。さらに、リージョンごとにランを分散させ、失敗時のリスクを軽減する設計を導入した。

items.titleJa: Modern Web Guidance のスキャンが 0 件でも、JS を 58 行減らせた
items.summaryJa: 公式の legacy-scan は 0 件だったが、ガイド趣旨に合う候補をテーマ切替、視覚的に隠すクラス、dvh/svh の 3 つに絞り適用。結果、JS 行数は 832 から 774 へ 58 行減り、Lighthouse の Performance は 92 から 94、TBT は 168ms から 33ms と改善したが、3 回計測の中央値比較のため確定的な改善とは言えない。適用後はテーマ処理を1か所へ集約し、視覚的に隠すクラスを clip から clip-path に置換、dvh/svh を実機確認後採用した。
